name: South Indian megalithic culture
title: The story of the South Indian megalithic culture

text: About 3,000 years ago, people in South India buried their dead in graves built or marked with big stones.
At one site, rice found in a burial urn with iron tools is more than 3,100 years old.
src: Hallur in Karnataka and Adichanallur in Tamil Nadu, more securely dated, are generally placed around 1000 BCE / an archaeologists’ label for an Iron Age way of burying the dead in graves built or marked with large stones, or in clay urns
c. 1248–1155 BCE: Rice from an intact burial urn holding iron artefacts at Sivagalai, Tamil Nadu, gives these dates

text: They used iron to make sickles for farming and spears and swords for fighting.
An iron furnace at Kodumanal, the oldest well-dated one in Tamil Nadu, is more than 2,400 years old.
src: used iron for farming tools such as sickles and for weapons such as spears, swords and arrowheads
5th century BCE: The earliest reliably dated iron furnace in Tamil Nadu is built at Kodumanal

text: The dead were laid in stone boxes or in pits ringed by boulders, with pots, iron tools and beads.
At Adichanallur, people were buried in big clay pots called urns.
src: In the megalithic period the dead were laid in stone cists or pits surrounded by a circle, or concentric circles, of boulders, with funeral pots, iron implements and beads
At Adichanallur skeletons were buried in clay urns

text: Many pots were scratched with symbols, and nobody knows for sure what they mean.
Later, writing called Tamil-Brahmi took the place of the old marks.
src: pots scratched with symbols whose meaning is still unknown
On the inscribed sherds, Brahmi and Tamil-Brahmi gradually replace the older marks

text: On Brahmagiri, a granite hill in Chitradurga, archaeologists, people who dig up the past, found a burial ground of 300 tombs.
Today a museum is planned at Adichanallur, and a museum at Keezhadi is to show burial urns.
src: Brahmagiri, a granite outcrop in Chitradurga district / At Brahmagiri a cemetery of 300 tombs
In 2023 the foundation stone was laid for an on-site museum at Adichanallur / the Keezhadi Heritage Museum, opened the same year, is to show urns from Konthagai
